segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's design a distributed rate limiter for a public API.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The first requirement is one hundred requests per minute for each normal client, and we also need a higher tier for partners who have signed a contract with us.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: So we need at least two policy tiers. Do we key the limit on the API key, the user identity, or the source IP address?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: I would key it on the API key as the primary identity, and fall back to the IP address only for unauthenticated endpoints like login and password reset.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: That makes sense. IP based limiting alone breaks badly behind corporate NAT, where thousands of users share a single egress address.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Right, and it also breaks for mobile carriers. One carrier gateway can front a huge population, so we would punish legitimate traffic.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's talk about the algorithm. The obvious starting point is a fixed window counter, one counter per key per minute.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Fixed windows are cheap and easy to reason about, but they allow a burst of double the limit at the window boundary.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Exactly. A client can send one hundred requests at the last second of one minute and another hundred at the first second of the next.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: For a public API that is a real problem, because the backend sees two hundred requests inside a two second span even though the policy says one hundred per minute.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The sliding window log fixes that precisely. We store a timestamp for every request and count the entries inside the trailing sixty seconds.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Precise, but expensive. For a key doing one hundred requests per minute we hold one hundred timestamps, and memory grows linearly with traffic.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: So the practical middle ground is the sliding window counter, where we blend the previous window and the current window using a weighted average.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That gives us accuracy within a small error margin while storing only two integers per key, which is a good trade for a high volume API.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: There is also the token bucket, which I like because it expresses burst capacity as a first class concept.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Agreed. The bucket holds a maximum number of tokens, tokens refill at a steady rate, and a request is allowed only if it can remove a token.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: So a client that has been quiet accumulates tokens and can send a short burst, which is usually what API consumers actually want.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We should cap the bucket so idle clients cannot accumulate an unlimited burst. Capacity of one hundred with a refill of one point six seven tokens per second matches our policy.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's move to the distributed part. We will run many stateless API gateway nodes, so the counter cannot live in local memory.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: If each node keeps its own counter, then with ten nodes a client effectively gets ten times the limit, assuming the load balancer spreads traffic evenly.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: So we need shared state. The standard choice is Redis, keyed by the client identifier and the window, with atomic increment operations.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We should do the whole check and decrement inside a single Lua script so the read, the compare and the write are atomic on the Redis side.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: That avoids the classic race where two gateway nodes both read ninety nine and both decide to allow the request.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: For the token bucket the script would compute the elapsed time since the last refill, add the earned tokens, clamp to capacity, then try to spend one.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We store the token count and the last refill timestamp in a single hash, so one round trip does the entire decision.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Latency budget matters here. Every request pays this cost, so we want the Redis call to stay in the low single digit milliseconds.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: That means the Redis cluster should be in the same region and ideally the same availability zone group as the gateway fleet.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We should also shard by key so a hot client does not concentrate all the load on one Redis primary.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Redis Cluster hashes the key to a slot, so as long as our key space is wide, the distribution is naturally balanced.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: But a single abusive client is still a single key, and a single key always lands on a single node. That is our hot key problem.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: For that case we can shard the counter itself, splitting the limit across a few sub counters and picking one at random per request.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That reduces contention at the cost of some accuracy, because the sub counters drift and one may exhaust before the others.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Another option for extreme traffic is a local token allocation model, where each gateway node leases a slice of the budget from Redis.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: So a node asks for ten tokens at a time, serves them locally without any network call, and goes back for more when the lease runs low.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: That cuts the Redis call rate by an order of magnitude, and the accuracy loss is bounded by the unspent leases at the moment of a burst.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Let's discuss failure handling. What happens when Redis is unreachable or slow beyond our timeout?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We need an explicit policy. Fail open means we allow the traffic and protect availability. Fail closed means we reject and protect the backend.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: For a public API I would fail open for normal endpoints, but fail closed for expensive or sensitive ones like account creation and bulk export.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We should also degrade to a local in memory limiter when the shared store is down, so there is still some ceiling rather than none at all.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Good. The local fallback should use a conservative limit, since each node enforces it independently and the effective total is multiplied by the fleet size.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Now the response contract. On rejection we return status four twenty nine, too many requests, with a Retry-After header.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And on every response we should include the limit, the remaining allowance and the reset timestamp, so well behaved clients can pace themselves.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Those headers turn the rate limiter from a punishment into a protocol. Clients can back off proactively instead of hammering and getting blocked.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We should also recommend jittered exponential backoff in the client documentation, otherwise every rejected client retries at the same reset instant.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: That synchronized retry storm is a real failure mode. Jitter spreads the recovery traffic instead of creating a second spike.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: What about rules configuration? I would keep the policies in a control plane and push them to the gateways, rather than hard coding them.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Yes, a policy service with versioned rules, so we can change a partner tier without a deployment. The gateways cache the rules and refresh periodically.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We should also support per endpoint overrides. A cheap read endpoint and an expensive search endpoint should not share the same budget.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: A weighted cost model handles that well. A search request spends five tokens while a simple read spends one.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: For observability we need metrics on allowed and rejected counts per tier, the top rejected keys, and the latency of the limiter itself.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We should alert when the rejection rate crosses a threshold, because that usually means either an attack or a client that shipped a bad loop.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: One more concern is multi region. If a client can hit two regions, do we enforce a global limit or a per region limit?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Cross region synchronous checks would add tens of milliseconds, so I would enforce per region budgets and reconcile asynchronously for billing.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That is a reasonable trade. The limiter protects capacity, which is regional anyway, and the exact global count only matters for the contract.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: So to summarize, token bucket in Redis with atomic Lua scripts, local leases for hot keys, explicit fail open policy, and standard headers.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Plus a versioned policy control plane, weighted endpoint costs, and per region enforcement. I think that covers the design end to end.
